hops.afterHeading: Hairy skin: two endings and the class table
hops.title: What fine arm hair is for
hops.text: Fine forearm hair does little to keep us warm, and it is often described as having no function at all. Isabelle Dean and Michael Siva-Jothy at the University of Sheffield tested another job for it. They shaved one forearm of each of 29 student volunteers, drew a Vaseline boundary on both arms, and set a hungry, paint-marked bed bug inside it. The volunteers looked away and clicked a tally counter whenever they felt something. Bugs were removed upon extending their mouthparts, before biting, or removed and excluded if five minutes passed first. Volunteers clicked more often on unshaved arms; on hairier unshaved arms, bugs took longer to extend their mouthparts.

sources.citation: Dean I & Siva-Jothy MT, Biology Letters 8(3):358–361 (2012), PMCID PMC3367735

image.caption: Volunteers felt bed bugs more often on unshaved arms; on hairier unshaved arms, bugs took longer to extend their mouthparts.

hops.afterHeading: Your own skin: human touch classes and C-tactile afferents
hops.title: Two years of recording from their own nerves
hops.text: Microneurography began in 1965 at the Academic Hospital in Uppsala, where Karl-Erik Hagbarth and Åke Vallbo set out to study muscle control in awake people. Animal work offered no playbook: nothing like a hand-guided tungsten electrode pushed through the skin into an intact nerve had been tried. For two years the two of them tested electrodes on their own nerves, watching for signs of damage. Temporary pins-and-needles were common; lasting injury never came. They expected only the blurred signal of many fibres at once, until small, regular blips on their film strips turned out to be single units. Every human touch class in this section rests on that surprise.

sources.citation: Vallbo AB & Hagbarth KE, Experimental Neurology 21(3):270–289 (1968), PMID 5673644
Vallbo ÅB, Journal of Neurophysiology 120(3):1415–1427 (2018), PMID 29924706

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage laboratory desk with a glowing oscilloscope, a wooden speaker and a notebook beside a snowy window.
image.caption: During two years of self-testing in Uppsala, Hagbarth and Vallbo unexpectedly spotted signals from single nerve fibres.

hops.afterHeading: How a tuning is built: direction
hops.title: Bat wing hairs that report airflow direction
hops.text: A bat's wing looks bare, but it carries microscopic hairs 100 to 600 micrometers long. Susanne Sterbing-D'Angelo and colleagues puffed air across the wings of big brown bats while recording from somatosensory cortex. The responses were direction-tuned, a bit like the mouse Aδ-LTMRs here, and along the trailing edge and midwing they favoured air coming from behind. Reversed flow like that appears when air separates from the wing, which may signal a stall. Two short-tailed fruit bats then had hairs removed from the upper wing surface and the underside's trailing edge. Their peak average flight speed rose from about 2.5 to 3.5 m/s, and their turns around obstacles grew wider.

sources.citation: Sterbing-D'Angelo S, Chadha M, Chiu C, Falk B, Xian W, Barcelo J, Zook JM & Moss CF, PNAS 108(27):11291–11296 (2011), PMCID PMC3131348
Sterbing-D'Angelo S, Chadha M, Chiu C, Falk B, Xian W, Barcelo J, Zook JM & Moss CF, PNAS 108(27):11291–11296 (2011), PMCID PMC3131348

audio.title: Bed bugs, elephant feet and the pace of a warm hand
audio.transcript:
Skin can turn one light touch into several separate reports at once, which can sound over-engineered. Why give one patch of skin vibration detectors, hair-bending sensors and slow stroking fibres all at the same time? Three studies show those channels earning their keep.

Start with the fine hair on your forearm. It does little to keep us warm, and scientists have often described it as having no function. Isabelle Dean and Michael Siva-Jothy at the University of Sheffield tested whether it works as an insect alarm. They recruited twenty-nine student volunteers, shaved one forearm, left the other alone, and drew a Vaseline fence on each arm. Then they placed a hungry female bed bug, marked with a small dot of acrylic paint, inside the fence while the volunteer looked away and clicked a tally counter every time they felt something. The researchers removed a bug when it extended its mouthparts, before it could bite, and removed and excluded any bug that had not done so after five minutes. Volunteers clicked significantly more often on the unshaved arm, and on hairier unshaved arms, bugs took longer to extend their mouthparts. The study did not measure hair deflection or identify which receptors fired, but one possible explanation is that a crawling insect can bend those fine hairs, and hair deflection can activate touch-sensitive afferents.

Now go from tiny hairs to elephant feet. In human skin, Pacinian corpuscles are most sensitive near two hundred and fifty hertz, but they respond across a range that reaches down to ten hertz. In two thousand and seven, Donna Bouley and colleagues examined the feet of Asian elephants and found Pacinian corpuscles packed in clusters of up to eighteen. In the forefoot slices they counted, fifty-two percent of the corpuscles sat in the front region; in the hindfoot slices, forty-seven percent sat in the rear region. Elephant rumbles of twenty to forty hertz travel through the ground as well as the air. In Namibia's Etosha National Park, African elephants responding to recorded rumbles played back through the ground have been seen to freeze, shift their weight onto their forefeet, or rock back onto the heels of their hind feet. The authors propose that loading those parts of the foot could help transmit vibrations to the corpuscle clusters inside the dermis and digital cushion, though their study did not measure how sensitive elephant corpuscles are.

Finally, what happens when the fast, myelinated touch lines go silent? In two thousand and two, Håkan Olausson and colleagues studied a rare patient who lacked the large myelinated fibres that carry discriminative touch. When the researchers stroked her hairy skin with a soft brush to engage the slow, unmyelinated C tactile fibres, she reported a faint, pleasant touch. Brain imaging showed activity in the insular cortex but not in the primary or secondary somatosensory areas. Later studies showed how closely those fibres match human contact. When volunteers were asked to stroke a partner or their baby, every one of them used speeds that can activate C tactile fibres, and they stroked more slowly than a separate group asked to stroke an artificial arm. And with slow stroking at three centimetres per second at eighteen, thirty-two or forty-two degrees Celsius, C tactile fibres gave their strongest mean response at thirty-two, typical skin temperature, while the four myelinated hair afferents directly compared showed no statistically significant temperature effect across the conditions tested.

Hair catches a crawling bug, clustered corpuscles may pick up a distant rumble, and slow unmyelinated fibres respond best to a gentle, warm hand. One touch is several reports at once.
